sources.citation: Dundaa, Mark Gandaa. 2013. Aspects of Birfor phonology. MPhil thesis, Department of Linguistics, University of Ghana, Legon. xxii+187 pp. (UGSpace handle 123456789/5375)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request); access check: not located online or in the libraries checked
sources.note: Nothing on word stress/accent placement. Ch.4 Tonology (pp.114-147): 'Bɩrfʊɔr is a tonal language' (p.116), three level tones H, L, M plus rising/falling contours, syllable is the TBU, lexical and grammatical tone, H-spread, downdrift etc. The word 'stress' appears only in generic definitions (diphthong nucleus = 'most stressed vowel', §2.1.7; Kenstowicz quote that the nucleus is 'the domain for the assignment of tone and stress', p.69), not as a claim about Birfor.

sources.citation: Kuch, Larry (Lawrence D.). 1993. The Phonology of Birifor. Collected Language Notes 21. Legon: Institute of African Studies, University of Ghana (for GILLBT). 37 pp. [Rosetta Project scans: detail (p.1), contents, phon (pp.2-27), references, vocab]
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request); access check: open copy online; also in print at Harvard (Widener Library, call number 2235.17.50 no. 21)
sources.note: No mention of stress or accent anywhere (inventory, contrasts, syllable structure, morpheme/word structure, distribution, ATR harmony). Introduction p.1: 'Tone has not been discussed in this paper; however, Birifor does have high and low phonemic tones. This has been covered in an unpublished manuscript by myself.' p.17: long vowels are two tone-bearing units (LH, HL contours only on long vowels).
Segment inventory only; no tones or stress information.
Vowel/consonant charts and orthography only; nothing on stress or tone; bibliography = Kuch 1993 (archive.org Rosetta link) and Dundaa 2013.
